fields.description: Which of the two inbound mechanisms delivered this. Interaction = the Chat app's HTTPS endpoint. Workspace Event = a Pub/Sub push from a Workspace Events subscription.
fields.label: Transport

fields.description: e.g. google.workspace.chat.message.v1.created, or MESSAGE. Deliberately not indexed - dedupe is on pubsub_message_id and on Chat Message.gchat_message_name, and a third probe would be redundant.
fields.label: Event Type

fields.description: Set from frappe.utils.now_datetime(), never from SQL NOW() - the site clock and the database clock are not guaranteed to be the same reading.
fields.label: Received At

fields.description: Processed and Ignored rows are purged by retention. Failed rows are never purged automatically: a purge that deletes the evidence of the events it failed to process is a purge that hides an outage.
fields.label: Status

fields.description: Failure retries only - a Google 5xx, a token mint that timed out, a room with nobody to read as. Compared against Chat Settings.relay_max_attempts by sync.inbound._fail_or_retry, and against nothing else.
fields.label: Attempts

fields.description: Defer budget spend, kept SEPARATE from attempts on purpose. A DEFER means an outbound write for this room is still in flight and we cannot yet tell our own echo from a coworker's message; a failed attempt means Google did not answer. Sharing one column made two unrelated ceilings eat each other - three defers left only two real retries before the row was marked Failed, and one transient messages.get timeout permanently shrank that event's defer budget. classify_inbound compares THIS against Chat Settings.echo_defer_budget.
fields.label: Defer Count

fields.description: Do not re-drive this row before this moment. A defer's delay has to be DURABLE or it is not a delay: frappe.enqueue exposes no way to reach RQ's scheduler, and RQ's own scheduling lives in the queue Redis a production deploy FLUSHDBs - so the previous 'delay_seconds' argument was dropped on the floor, a DEFER re-enqueued instantly, and three defers burned the whole echo_defer_budget in milliseconds while waiting out nothing. sweep_stuck_inbound_events honours this column, which makes the sweeper's cron interval the real defer granularity (it is scheduled every minute for exactly that reason). Empty is the normal state: a Pub/Sub-delivered row has never asked to wait, and the sweeper treats empty as 'eligible once received_at is older than STUCK_EVENT_MINUTES'.
fields.label: Available At

fields.description: What this delivery produced, if anything. A batched payload produces many message operations from one row, so this points at the first or only one.
fields.label: Resulting Message

fields.description: spaces/{space} - resolved to a Chat Room by the worker.
fields.label: Google Space Name

fields.description: The changed resource named by the event.
fields.label: Google Resource Name

fields.description: Pub/Sub's own message id. Pub/Sub is at-least-once, so this unique constraint is the whole duplicate defence: the second delivery of the same message becomes a DuplicateEntryError the puller treats as 'already acked'. Empty for the HTTP transport - Frappe coerces empty to NULL on a unique DocField, and MariaDB allows unlimited NULLs in a unique index, so those rows do not collide with each other.
fields.label: Pub/Sub Message ID

fields.description: The event body VERBATIM, stored before any interpretation. Never normalised, never re-serialised, never trimmed. This column is the only way to reprocess after a parser bug, the fixture source for the parser's own tests, and the only evidence available when Google changes a payload shape - which they do. Batched payloads (batchCreated, batchUpdated, batchDeleted, batchChanged) are the norm, and one row is one delivery, not one contained resource, so acknowledging the delivery stays a single decision.
fields.label: Payload
